title: VCE Applied Computing: Software Development, Units 3 and 4

areas.title: Software development: programming
areas.assessment: School-assessed coursework: four teacher-designed programming modules, at least two with a GUI
areas.summary: Interpret requirements and designs, then write, validate, debug and test modules in a programming language.

areas.title: Software development: analysis and design
areas.summary: Analyse a need or opportunity, plan the project, document requirements in an SRS, and generate and evaluate designs.

areas.title: Software development: development and evaluation
areas.summary: Develop and test the designed solution, evaluate it, and assess how well the project plan worked.

areas.title: Cyber security: secure software development practices
areas.summary: Evaluate how an organisation develops software, identify security risks, and recommend controls and improvements.

groups.title: Terms used in this study
groups.summary: The study design's Terms used in this study. The exam uses these definitions, and every term is examinable.

groups.title: Problem-solving methodology
groups.summary: The four stages (analysis, design, development, evaluation), their activities, and the problem-solving methodology specifications.

kks.title: AI in programming
kks.summary: Emerging uses of AI in programming: generating code from prompts, automated debugging and testing of modules, code optimisation, and using AI tools responsibly and ethically.
examples: A prompt that names the language, the inputs and the labelled outputs
An IDE tool that flags a likely error as code is typed
Reviewing AI-generated code before using it

kks.title: Requirements, constraints and scope
kks.summary: The characteristics of functional and non-functional requirements, constraints and scope, as read from the requirements a module is built to.
examples: Functional: the module calculates the total fee
Non-functional: results appear within two seconds
Constraint: the program must run offline

kks.title: Design tools for modules
kks.summary: Data dictionaries, mock-ups, object descriptions, input-process-output (IPO) charts and pseudocode as ways to represent a module before it is coded.
examples: A data dictionary with each item's name and data type
An object description listing attributes and methods
An IPO chart with Input, Processes and Output columns

kks.title: Data types
kks.summary: The characteristics of text (character, string), numeric (integer, floating point, date/time) and Boolean data types, and choosing the right one for each item of data.
examples: A single-letter grade stored as a character
A phone number stored as a string
A date of birth stored as date/time

kks.title: Data structures
kks.summary: One-dimensional arrays, two-dimensional arrays and records (fields of varying data types, reached by a field index): how each is organised and when each suits.
examples: A 1D array of scores indexed by integer
A 2D array indexed by row and column
A record with named fields of different types

kks.title: Data sources
kks.summary: Plain text (TXT), delimited (CSV) and XML files: how each is structured and the reasons for using each.
examples: A log written as plain text lines
A CSV export from a spreadsheet
An XML file whose tags describe each value

kks.title: Principles of OOP
kks.summary: Abstraction, encapsulation, generalisation and inheritance as the principles of object-oriented programming.
examples: A Vehicle superclass generalising Car and Truck
Private attributes reached only through the class's methods
Showing other code only what it needs to use

kks.title: Features of a programming language
kks.summary: Local and global variables and constants; data types; instructions and control structures (sequence, selection, iteration); arithmetic, logical and conditional operators; graphical user interfaces; functions and methods; classes and objects.

kks.title: Naming conventions
kks.summary: Why naming conventions are used, and how Hungarian notation, camel casing and snake casing name variables, interface controls and code structures.

kks.title: Validation
kks.summary: Existence (presence), type and range checking of data.

kks.title: Internal documentation
kks.summary: Why code carries internal documentation: to explain and justify data and code structures, to support code maintenance, and to leave placeholder comments (stubs) for future development.
examples: A comment justifying a binary search over a linear one
Comments that help a later developer maintain a module
A stub marking a method still to be written

kks.title: Sorting and searching
kks.summary: Selection sort, quick sort, binary search and linear search: how each works and how they compare.
examples: Quick sort is usually faster than selection sort on large lists

kks.title: Types of errors
kks.summary: Syntax, logic and runtime errors, including the runtime errors overflow, index out of range, type mismatch and divide by zero.
examples: Reading element 10 of a 10-element zero-based array

kks.title: Debugging and testing
kks.summary: Breakpoints, debugging statements, constructing relevant test data, and test cases that compare expected and actual output in testing tables.
examples: Setting a breakpoint inside a loop
A debugging statement that prints a variable's value
Boundary test data in a testing table

kks.title: Why software projects happen
kks.summary: Why individuals and organisations undertake software development projects: to increase productivity and efficiency, reduce costs, address a gap in the market, or meet organisational objectives or needs.
examples: Automating a paper booking process to save staff time
An app for a need no competitor serves

kks.title: The project brief
kks.summary: What a brief documents: an outline of the problem, need or opportunity, the proposed users, the programming languages to be used, feasibility and originality.
examples: Whether the project can be done with the time and skills available

kks.title: Gantt charts
kks.summary: Project management with Gantt charts: identifying, sequencing and allocating time to tasks, dependencies, milestones, the critical path, and monitoring and documenting progress.
examples: A task that can't start until testing ends
The longest chain of dependent tasks

kks.title: Data collection methods
kks.summary: Interviews, observations, surveys and reports as methods for collecting data to determine needs and requirements, and choosing one to suit the people and the detail needed.

kks.title: Functional and non-functional requirements
kks.summary: What the solution must do, and the qualities it must have.

kks.title: Constraints
kks.summary: Economic, legal, social and technical constraints that influence how a solution is developed.
examples: Economic: a fixed budget or deadline
Technical: must run on existing tablets

kks.title: Scope
kks.summary: The solution's scope: the boundaries of the solution or version, including what it will not do.
examples: The app will take bookings but will not process payments

kks.title: Analytical tools
kks.summary: Context diagrams (Level 0), data flow diagrams (Level 1) and use case diagrams: their components and the rules for drawing them.

kks.title: Software requirements specification
kks.summary: The purpose and features of an SRS: requirements, constraints, scope, user characteristics, technical environments, and analytical tools that depict existing processes and systems.
examples: The hardware and software the solution must run on

kks.title: Legal requirements
kks.summary: Key legal requirements for intellectual property and the ownership and privacy of data: the Copyright Act 1968, the Privacy Act 1988 (APPs 1, 3, 6, 8, 9 and 11) and the Privacy and Data Protection Act 2014 (IPPs 1, 2, 4, 5, 7, 9 and 10).
examples: Collecting only the personal information needed

kks.title: File management
kks.summary: Naming conventions, version control, backups (full, incremental, differential), security and disposal as techniques for managing project files.

kks.title: Ideation
kks.summary: Mood boards, brainstorming, mind maps, sketches and annotations as techniques and tools for generating design ideas.

kks.title: Evaluation criteria
kks.summary: Criteria for evaluating design ideas and the efficiency and effectiveness of solutions.

kks.title: Design tools for solutions
kks.summary: Data dictionaries, mock-ups, object descriptions, IPO charts and pseudocode for turning design ideas into detailed solution designs.
examples: A data dictionary for every variable and control
An annotated mock-up of each screen

kks.title: User experience
kks.summary: Affordance, interoperability, security (authentication and data protection) and usability as characteristics of user experience, and how each affects software design.
examples: Exporting to a format another system reads
A login before private data is shown

kks.title: Design principles
kks.summary: Alignment, balance, contrast, space, text formatting, usability and navigation as principles that shape a user interface's appearance and functionality.

kks.title: Efficient and effective solutions
kks.summary: What makes a solution efficient and effective, including user-centred design, clear and concise code, and detailed internal documentation.

kks.title: Data for input, storage and output
kks.summary: Choosing data types, data structures and data sources for input, storage and output.
examples: Reading a CSV into an array of records
Writing results to an XML file

kks.title: Language features in development
kks.summary: The programming language features used to build the solution (as in U3O1-KK08), plus access modifiers: public, protected and private.
examples: A private attribute only the class's own methods change
A protected attribute a subclass can use

kks.title: Established and innovative approaches
kks.summary: Code repositories, application programming interfaces (APIs) and libraries, and AI-based assistants as approaches to developing software.
examples: A shared repository with commit history
A mapping API instead of writing map code
An AI assistant suggesting the next line

kks.title: Validation techniques
kks.summary: Existence, type and range checking applied in the developed solution.
examples: Existence, type and range checks on a booking form

kks.title: Debugging and alpha testing
kks.summary: Breakpoints, commenting out code, relevant test data, and test cases comparing expected and actual output in testing tables, used to check that a solution meets requirements and works correctly.
examples: Commenting out a block to isolate a fault
Testing each module against a testing table

kks.title: Beta testing
kks.summary: Strategies for beta testing: constructing a testing plan and test scenarios, observing users as they work through the scenarios, and documenting the results.
examples: Choosing testers from the intended users
A scenario that walks through a booking
Recording what testers did and said

kks.title: Evaluation strategies
kks.summary: The features of an evaluation strategy: the evaluation criteria, the time frame, and who is responsible.
examples: Survey users two weeks after launch, run by the project manager

kks.title: Applying evaluation criteria
kks.summary: Techniques for applying evaluation criteria to judge a solution's efficiency and effectiveness.
examples: Timing how long a task takes

kks.title: Project plan disruptions
kks.summary: Factors that affect how effective a project plan is: scope creep, personnel changes and technical issues.
examples: The client adds a feature mid-project

kks.title: Recording progress
kks.summary: Recording a project's progress through adjustments to tasks and time frames, annotations to the project plan, and logs or journals.
examples: Annotating a Gantt chart with actual dates

kks.title: Assessing the project plan
kks.summary: Assessing how effective a project plan was by reviewing how many changes were made, why they were needed, and how they affected completing the project.
examples: Counting the changes made to the plan

kks.title: Organisational goals and objectives
kks.summary: The goals and objectives of medium and large organisations.
examples: An objective to cut processing time by 20% this year

kks.title: In-house versus external development
kks.summary: Advantages and disadvantages of developing software in-house or externally.
examples: In-house keeps control of the code
External brings expertise but less control

kks.title: Vulnerabilities and risks
kks.summary: Vulnerabilities and risks in insecure development environments: APIs, malware, unpatched software, poor identity and access management, man-in-the-middle attacks, insider threats, cyber security incidents, software acquired from third parties, ineffective code review, and combined development, testing and production environments.
examples: Development, testing and production sharing one environment
An insider misconfiguration exposing code and data

kks.title: Security controls
kks.summary: Controls that protect development practices and stored data: version control and code repositories, robust identity and access management, encryption, code review, regular updates and patches, and separate development, testing and production environments.

kks.title: Threat modelling
kks.summary: The principles of threat modelling: defining security requirements, identifying and mitigating threats, and confirming the threats have been mitigated.

kks.title: Evaluating security of development practices
kks.summary: Criteria for evaluating how secure an organisation's software development practices are.
examples: Is access limited to what each person needs?

kks.title: Legislation and frameworks
kks.summary: The Copyright Act 1968, the Essential Eight, the Information Security Manual's Guidelines for Software Development, the Privacy Act 1988 (APPs 1, 6, 8, 9 and 11) and the Privacy and Data Protection Act 2014 (IPPs 1, 2, 4, 5 and 9).

kks.title: Ethical issues
kks.summary: Ethical issues that arise in software development: ineffective security practices, using AI during development, intellectual property and copyright.

kks.title: Reducing threats and risks
kks.summary: Measures that reduce or remove threats, vulnerabilities and risks in organisations and development environments.

kks.title: Strategies for improving security
kks.summary: Onboarding or induction and developer training focused on secure development, and risk management plans, as strategies for improving the security of development practices.
examples: Security in the induction for new staff
